lessons.title: How does a touchscreen know where I touched?
lessons.subtitle: Electricity at your fingertip

scenes.title: Glass with a secret
scenes.narration: Your phone's screen looks like a plain piece of glass, but it is hiding a secret. Under the glass there is a grid of very thin wires, so thin you cannot see them. They are switched on all the time, waiting. Touch the screen with your finger, and something changes right under your skin.

draw.s: a grid of wires hides under the glass

scenes.title: A grid of tiny wires
scenes.narration: The wires run across and up the screen, like the lines in a maths book. Where one across wire crosses one up wire, the phone knows exactly one spot. When your finger touches, it feels the change at that crossing. That is how it knows where you touched.

draw.s: where they cross, the phone knows

scenes.title: Your finger is electric
scenes.narration: Your body is full of tiny electric charges. When your finger comes close, it steals a little electricity from the wires underneath. The phone notices that tiny dip. It is not pressure, and it is not heat — it is your own electricity saying I am here.

draw.s: a tiny dip in the wires

scenes.title: The chip reads the spot
scenes.narration: A tiny chip at the edge of the screen checks every crossing, thousands of times a second. The moment one changes, it sends two numbers to the phone: this far across, this far up. The phone turns those numbers into a tap, a swipe or a letter.

scenes.title: Why gloves do not work
scenes.narration: That is also why a touchscreen ignores a pencil, or your finger in thick winter gloves. They do not carry your electricity. Your skin does. So the next time you tap, remember: you are not pressing a button, you are completing a tiny electric conversation.

quiz.question: What does a touchscreen feel when your finger touches it?
quiz.explanation: The wires notice a small dip in electricity caused by your finger.

quiz.question: Why does a pencil not work on a touchscreen?
options: It does not carry your electricity
quiz.explanation: The screen needs your body's electricity to notice a touch.

quiz.question: What does the chip send to the phone?
quiz.explanation: One number for across and one for up tells the phone exactly where you touched.

lessons.title: How does soap wash dirt away?
lessons.subtitle: A tadpole that hugs grease

scenes.title: Water alone is not enough
scenes.narration: Wash your hands with water alone and something odd happens. The water rolls over the dirt instead of grabbing it, because oil and water refuse to mix. Your skin makes oil, and dirt sticks to that oil. Water slides past both of them. Soap is the clever thing that introduces them.

draw.s: water slides right past the grease

scenes.title: A tadpole with two ends
scenes.narration: A soap molecule is tiny, and it has two ends. One end loves water. The other end loves oil and grease. Imagine a tadpole with a water-loving head and an oil-loving tail. When you rub soap on wet hands, millions of these tadpoles swim towards the dirt.

draw.s: millions of these are in one drop

scenes.title: They wrap up the grease
scenes.narration: The tails dive into the grease and hold on. The heads stay out in the water. Together they wrap the grease into a tiny ball, with the dirt trapped inside and the water-friendly heads on the outside. Now the water is happy to carry it.

draw.s: a ball with clean water outside

scenes.title: Water carries it away
scenes.narration: When you rinse, the water grabs those little balls and washes them down the drain. The grease goes with them, even though water and grease still do not like each other. The soap did the introductions.

scenes.title: Bubbles are a bonus
scenes.narration: Soap also traps air, which is why you get bubbles — thin skins of soap with air inside. But the real job is smaller than a bubble: it is millions of tiny tadpoles, carrying dirt away.

draw.s: but the real work is too small to see

quiz.question: Why does water alone not clean greasy hands?
options: Water and oil do not mix
quiz.explanation: Oil and water push each other away, so the water cannot grab the grease.

quiz.question: What are the two ends of a soap molecule like?
options: A water-loving head and an oil-loving tail
quiz.explanation: One end holds water, the other holds grease — that is what joins them.

quiz.question: What happens when you rinse?
options: The grease stays on your hands
Water carries the soap balls away
quiz.explanation: The water-friendly outsides let water carry the grease down the drain.

lessons.title: Why does popcorn pop?
lessons.subtitle: A pressure cooker the size of a seed

scenes.title: Water in a hard shell
scenes.narration: A popcorn kernel looks like a hard little seed. Inside it there is a tiny plant, and around the plant there is a drop of water. The outside is a shell so tough that the water cannot get out, even when it gets hot.

draw.s: a tough shell keeps it in

scenes.title: The steam pushes
scenes.narration: Put the kernel in a hot pan. The water inside turns into steam, and steam takes up much more room than water. The steam pushes and pushes against the shell. The shell holds on, and the pressure builds like a tiny balloon inside a suit of armour.

scenes.title: The shell cracks open
scenes.narration: Then the shell cracks! The steam escapes all at once, and the soft starch inside puffs out and turns crispy. That is the pop you hear — it is steam breaking free. The white part is the plant's food, cooked in a second.

draw.s: starch puffs into a fluffy cloud

scenes.title: Why rice does not pop
scenes.narration: Rice and wheat have shells that are too strong, or not enough water inside, so they do not explode. Popcorn is special: just the right shell and just the right amount of water.

draw.s: the right shell, the right water

scenes.title: The pop is steam
scenes.narration: So a popcorn kernel is a tiny pressure cooker. Heat the water, trap the steam, and wait for the shell to give up. The pop is not the kernel shouting — it is steam saying hello.

quiz.question: What is inside a popcorn kernel?
quiz.explanation: Water inside the kernel turns to steam when it gets hot.

quiz.question: What pushes the shell open?
quiz.explanation: Steam takes far more room than water, so it pushes from inside.

quiz.question: Why does rice not pop like popcorn?
options: Its shell is too strong or too dry
quiz.explanation: Popcorn has just the right shell and just the right amount of water.

lessons.title: Why does a mirror show me?
lessons.subtitle: Light that bounces back

scenes.title: Light bounces
scenes.narration: Light travels in straight lines, until it hits something. When it hits a smooth, shiny surface, it bounces off, and it bounces at the same angle it arrived. That is reflection, and it is the whole trick behind a mirror.

draw.s: light bounces off a smooth surface

scenes.title: Why a wall is not a mirror
scenes.narration: A rough wall bounces light in every direction, so the light that reaches your eye is a jumble — no picture. A mirror is so smooth that all the light from one spot bounces to one place, and your eye can put the picture back together.

draw.s: a rough wall scatters the light

scenes.title: Glass, silver, paint
scenes.narration: A mirror is not just glass. Behind the glass there is a thin layer of shiny metal, usually silver, and behind that a coat of paint. Light passes through the glass, bounces off the silver, and comes back to you.

scenes.title: Front to back
scenes.narration: But why does a mirror seem to swap left and right? It does not. It swaps front and back. Your reflection's nose points at your nose. Raise your right hand, and the reflection raises the hand on your right side — the one that looks like its left.

scenes.title: Smooth and clean
scenes.narration: So a mirror is a light bouncer with a silver back. Keep it clean and smooth, and it will hand your own picture back to you, front to back, every time.

quiz.question: What does light do on a smooth, shiny surface?
options: Bounces off at the same angle
quiz.explanation: That bouncing is called reflection — it is how mirrors work.

quiz.question: Why can you see a picture in a mirror but not in a wall?
options: A rough wall scatters light everywhere
quiz.explanation: A smooth surface sends light from one spot to one place, so a picture forms.

quiz.question: What does a mirror really swap?
quiz.explanation: It swaps front and back — your reflection's nose points at your nose.
